chunks: And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said:
I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about women: is ghusl of Friday upon them? He said: “Yes.”

So if someone says: how do you use these reports as evidence while they imply that ghusl of Friday is obligatory, whereas according to you it is a sunnah (prophetic tradition), not an obligation? We say: what these reports contain of the wording of obligation is intended to mean that it is more appropriate for a person to do it. A thing may be called obligatory when doing it is more fitting, and what indicates this interpretation is that what is intended is not the obligation that it is never permissible to leave under any circumstance.

key_terms.الْفَرْضَ: the binding obligation that may not be omitted
key_terms.الْوُجُوبِ: the wording or indication of obligation in the reports
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: a recommended prophetic tradition rather than a binding duty
key_terms.غُسْلُ الْجُمُعَةِ: the ritual bath associated with Friday
key_terms.فَرِيضَةٍ: a strictly obligatory act established as binding
key_terms.وَاجِبٌ: described here in the sense of emphasized performance, not necessarily strict legal obligation

ai.seo_question: Is Friday ghusl obligatory for women in Shia hadith, or is it a recommended sunnah (prophetic tradition)?
ai.summary: This report states that women are included in the recommendation of ghusl for Friday. The accompanying discussion clarifies that reports using the language of wujub here are understood to indicate emphasized sunnah (prophetic tradition) and priority, not a strictly binding legal obligation whose omission is forbidden in all circumstances.
